constraints: The input is a tree rather than a DAG with shared child nodes.
Per-node local work is O(1).
h denotes tree height in nodes.

blocks.text: Each non-null call owns one distinct real node and creates calls only for that node's children. In a tree, no child has two parents, so no non-null state is recomputed. There are n non-null calls and O(n) null-child calls, yielding O(n) time. During depth-first execution, at most one root-to-current path is active, giving O(h) stack space. A full tree can have roughly 2^h nodes, but that is still linear in n; expressing cost in height does not justify calling it exponential in the input size n.

messages.text: The base is reached through a number of calls proportional to the tree's nodes and null edges; terminal values do not erase traversal work.

feedback.reason: The recursion follows disjoint child ownership, so total calls scale with actual nodes while simultaneous frames scale with height.

blocks.text: Empty ranges are not the only atomic inputs for sorting: a one-element range is already sorted. With hi - lo == 1, mid equals lo. The first child is empty and returns, but the second child is [lo, hi), exactly the parent state. The correct terminal region is hi - lo <= 1. This is a high-value boundary diagnosis because the code visibly contains an empty base and a conventional split, yet the reachable singleton state violates strict progress.

The broader diagnostic rule is that progress assumptions belong to the actual traversed graph, not to a label such as “directory tree.” A visible None base does not guarantee that every path reaches None.

blocks.text: Diagnose recursive code in dependency order. The base contract for single-digit values is coherent, and n % 10 is the correct local contribution for a digit sum. But the transition digitSum(n) does not remove the last digit; the state graph contains a self-loop at every n >= 10. Therefore no recursive result is ever available to add. A precise review should name the earliest broken contract—progress on state—rather than proposing unrelated base, combination, or complexity changes.
